KECGrounding.section1Title: ⚡ What is the KEC Grounding & Protective Conductor Sizing Calculator?
KECGrounding.section1Para1: The KEC Grounding & Protective Conductor Sizing Calculator is a free online tool that quickly and accurately calculates the minimum cross-sectional area for grounding and protective conductors according to Article 142.3.2 of the Korea Electrical Code (KEC). It is designed for immediate use in various professional environments including electrical construction sites, design offices, supervision work, and electrical safety inspections.
KECGrounding.section1Para2: Grounding and protective conductors are critical safety devices in electrical installations, preventing electric shock accidents and fires. KEC regulations strictly define the minimum thickness of these conductors based on either the phase conductor cross-sectional area or fault current and interruption time. This calculator supports both methods.
KECGrounding.section1Para3: All calculations are processed instantly in your browser, providing not only the theoretical minimum value but also automatically recommending the most appropriate standard cable size (1.5SQ to 300SQ) available on the market. Access it quickly from anywhere on smartphones, tablets, or PCs for immediate on-site verification.
KECGrounding.useCase1Desc: Instantly verify grounding conductor size and order materials during wiring design for new buildings or remodeling projects.
KECGrounding.useCase2Desc: Quickly review KEC compliance when designing protective conductors and conducting safety inspections for high-voltage, high-current equipment.
KECGrounding.useCase3Desc: Real-time verification of grounding conductor specifications against regulations during design drawing preparation and field supervision.
KECGrounding.useCase4Desc: Used as a learning tool for electrical certification exam preparation (Electrician, Industrial Engineer, Professional Engineer) and electrical engineering students.
KECGrounding.step1Desc: Choose between phase conductor cross-section (table method) or fault current (formula method) tabs.
KECGrounding.step2Desc: Input phase conductor cross-section (㎟), or fault current (A), interruption time (sec), and material factor (k).
KECGrounding.step3Desc: The theoretical minimum cross-section and the final recommended standard cable size are prominently displayed.
KECGrounding.step4Desc: Order materials or reflect the recommended size in drawings. Consult a qualified electrical engineer if necessary.
KECGrounding.faq1A: KEC (Korea Electrical Code) Article 142 covers protection against electric shock in low-voltage electrical installations. Article 142.3.2 specifically defines the method for calculating minimum cross-sectional area of protective and grounding conductors, presenting both a table based on phase conductor cross-section and a formula based on fault current (S = √(I²t) / k).
KECGrounding.faq2Q: Can I use a larger cable than the calculated value?
KECGrounding.faq2A: Yes, absolutely. KEC regulations specify 'minimum' requirements, so using thicker cables for safety margin is recommended. Considering future expansion possibilities and voltage drop, selecting a generous size is advantageous.
KECGrounding.faq3Q: How do I select the k factor?
KECGrounding.faq3A: The k factor is determined by conductor material (Copper Cu / Aluminum Al) and insulation type (PVC / XLPE). Most building wiring uses Cu-PVC (k=115), while high-temperature environments or high-power equipment often use Cu-XLPE (k=143). Check the cable specification sheet to select the accurate value.
KECGrounding.faq4Q: Which method should I use - phase conductor or fault current?
KECGrounding.faq4A: Generally, the phase conductor cross-section method (table calculation) is simpler and more commonly used in low-voltage wiring design. The fault current method is used when interruption time and fault current values are accurately known, mainly for high-voltage equipment or special environments. Both methods are accurate according to KEC regulations.
KECGrounding.faq5Q: Can I use the results from this tool in official design drawings?
KECGrounding.faq5A: While this tool accurately reflects KEC regulations, official design drawings must be reviewed and approved by a qualified electrical engineer (Professional Engineer or higher). Consider it a reference tool as additional factors such as site conditions, environmental factors, and related regulations may apply.

AquariumBioload.section1Para1: The Aquarium Bioload Calculator is a free online tool for both beginners and experienced aquarists. Enter your tank size, fish species, and quantities to calculate real-time bioload and prevent overcrowding while creating optimal living conditions.
AquariumBioload.section1Para2: Bioload refers to the amount of waste produced by fish, which is a critical factor in water quality management. Excessive bioload rapidly increases ammonia, nitrite, and nitrate levels, harming fish health and potentially leading to fatalities.
AquariumBioload.section1Para3: This calculator features a database of over 15 popular aquarium fish species, considering factors such as bioload per fish, minimum tank size, optimal temperature range, temperament (peaceful/aggressive), and minimum schooling numbers to provide smart alerts.

AquariumBioload.faq1A: Bioload is the total amount of waste produced by organisms (mainly fish) in the aquarium. This includes feces, uneaten food, and ammonia from respiration, all of which directly impact water quality. Proper bioload management is essential for maintaining a healthy aquarium.
AquariumBioload.faq2Q: What should I do if the calculator shows over 100%?
AquariumBioload.faq2A: Over 100% indicates overcrowding, which can lead to poor water quality and fish stress. Solutions include: 1) upgrading to a larger tank, 2) reducing fish quantity, 3) installing a more powerful filtration system, or 4) increasing water change frequency (2-3 times weekly).
AquariumBioload.faq3Q: Why is the minimum schooling number important?
AquariumBioload.faq3A: Schooling fish like neon tetras, rasboras, and zebra danios have natural instincts to live in groups. Keeping them alone or in small numbers causes severe stress. They must be kept in groups of at least the recommended minimum to display natural behaviors and remain healthy.
AquariumBioload.faq4Q: Can I keep aggressive and peaceful fish together?
AquariumBioload.faq4A: Generally not recommended. Aggressive species like bettas and cichlids may attack or nip the fins of peaceful species like guppies and neon tetras. If attempting a community tank, provide ample hiding spots and space while closely monitoring individual behavior.

BubblePopart.about_title: How the bubble lettering is drawn
BubblePopart.about: Each letter is painted on its own: first a thick outer outline, then an optional inner outline, then the fill color, and finally two small white highlight dots near the top left. Because the next letter's outline lands on top of the previous letter's fill, tightening the letter spacing below 1.0 makes the letters overlap like a bunch of balloons, while widening it above 1.0 gives a cleaner signboard look. The 3D depth effect stacks ten slightly shifted copies of each letter in a darker shade, and the shadow option offsets a single copy. On a dark background a near-black outline would disappear, so it is drawn in white automatically. The preview and the download use the same drawing function at different scales, so the file matches what you see.

Neon — glowing letters on a dark night-sky gradient. Great for night events and game thumbnails.

faq.q: Will long text get cut off at the edges?
faq.a: No. If the letters, outlines, shadows, and decorations together exceed 94% of the image, the font size is reduced automatically so everything sits inside a 3% margin. The caption under the preview then shows the size actually used, for example "scaled down to 72px". Twenty characters on three lines at the largest size fit the same way.

faq.q: Is the quality good enough for printing?
faq.a: It depends on the export scale. A4 at 1× is 794×1123 pixels, about 96 dpi on paper, which is really screen quality. At 3× it becomes 2382×3369 pixels, about 288 dpi, close to the usual 300 dpi print standard. Choose 3× for anything you print, and check with your print shop before going to A3 or larger.

faq.q: How do I make a transparent PNG?
faq.a: Choose Transparent under Background. Only the letters and decorations are saved, and everything else becomes transparent in the PNG. The grey checkerboard in the preview just marks transparent areas and is not part of the file. Turning on the sticker border keeps the text readable on both light and dark surfaces.

faq.q: Can I use the images commercially?
faq.a: Yes. All six fonts are SIL Open Font License fonts from Google Fonts, so the images may be used in shop promotions, product packaging, and paid content. The license only forbids selling the font files on their own. You are still responsible for the rights to the words or brand names you put in the image.

faq.q: Why did my black outline turn white?
faq.a: A near-black outline on a dark background blends into it and the letters lose their shape. When the background is dark, the tool therefore draws a black outline in white automatically and shows a note under the Outline section. Outlines in other colors are left as chosen, so pick a color yourself if you want something different.

SmartExcelMapper.seoTitle: Convert report-style Excel files into a database list in a few clicks
SmartExcelMapper.seoPara1: Purchase orders, quotes and inventory reports usually arrive as formatted reports: a title block, merged cells, a few lines of order details and then the item table. Getting that into a database or a pivot table normally means copying and pasting by hand. With this tool you only tell it which row holds the column names (for example row 6) and where the data starts (row 7); it then turns the sheet into a clean list with one record per row.
SmartExcelMapper.seoPara2: Example: the top of a purchase order shows 'Date: 2026-03-21' and 'Supplier: Daehan Trading'. Click those cells and name the output columns 'Order date' and 'Customer' — the values are copied into every item row automatically (broadcasting). Repeating data such as item name and quantity is mapped with one click on its column header. Whether the sheet has 100 rows or 1,000, the conversion takes a few seconds.
SmartExcelMapper.seoPara3: All processing runs in your browser, so the file is never uploaded to a server. You can convert sheets that contain sensitive business data with peace of mind.
SmartExcelMapper.faq1Q: What is the header row number?
SmartExcelMapper.faq1A: It is the number of the row in your Excel file that contains the column names. If row 6 reads [No. | Item code | Item name | Quantity], the header row is 6. Company reports often have a title or date in rows 1–5 and the column names further down.
SmartExcelMapper.faq2Q: When should I use fixed-value broadcasting?
SmartExcelMapper.faq2A: Use it when a value such as the order date, customer name or person in charge appears only once at the top of the file but should be repeated on every item row. One click on the cell copies it to all rows, whether there are 10 or 1,000.
SmartExcelMapper.faq3Q: I added a wrong rule by mistake. What do I do?
SmartExcelMapper.faq3A: Press the 'Remove' button to the right of the rule and it is deleted immediately. You can change the rules at any time before downloading.
SmartExcelMapper.faq4Q: Is my data sent to a server?
SmartExcelMapper.faq4A: No. Everything runs in your browser on your own computer, and the file never leaves it. Nothing is uploaded or stored on our servers.
SmartExcelMapper.faq5Q: Will the result contain empty rows?
SmartExcelMapper.faq5A: No. Completely empty rows after the data start row are removed automatically, so the downloaded list contains only real records.
SmartExcelMapper.faq6Q: What happens if the workbook has several sheets?
SmartExcelMapper.faq6A: At the moment only the first sheet is read. To convert another sheet, move it to the first position in Excel and upload the file again.

AlbaPay.title: Korea Part-time Pay & Weekly Holiday Allowance Calculator {year}
AlbaPay.subtitle: For part-timers and employers in Korea — {year} minimum wage {wage}/hour. Weekly holiday allowance (juhyu sudang), weekly and monthly pay, and take-home pay.
AlbaPay.meta_title: Korea Part-time Pay Calculator {year} – Weekly Holiday Allowance (Juhyu) | Utility Hub
AlbaPay.meta_description: Calculate part-time pay in Korea with the {year} minimum wage of {wage}/hour: weekly holiday allowance (juhyu sudang), weekly and monthly pay, overtime and night premiums, and take-home pay after the 4 insurances or 3.3%.
AlbaPay.description: This calculator is for foreign part-timers and small business owners who need to check pay under Korean labour law. Enter an hourly wage and your hours and it shows the weekly holiday allowance (주휴수당, juhyu sudang), weekly pay, pay converted to a month, and take-home pay after the four social insurances or the 3.3% freelancer withholding. The {year} minimum wage of {wage} an hour is filled in for you, and you can switch the year to check last year's pay. Anyone contracted for 15 hours or more a week earns an extra paid day off each week worth (weekly hours ÷ 40) × 8 hours of pay, so a 40-hour week becomes 209 paid hours a month, or {monthly}. The weekly schedule tab takes start and end times and breaks for each day, splits out overtime and night work between 10 pm and 6 am, and handles shifts that end after midnight such as 6 pm to 2 am. Workplaces with five or more staff must add 50% for overtime, night and holiday work; smaller ones pay no premiums but still owe the weekly holiday allowance. Wages below the legal minimum are flagged in red. Everything runs in your browser and nothing you type is sent anywhere.
AlbaPay.about_title: What is the weekly holiday allowance (juhyu sudang)?
AlbaPay.about: Korean law gives every worker one paid day off a week, called juhyu (주휴), as long as they were contracted for at least 15 hours that week and showed up on every scheduled day. Part-timers and students qualify on exactly the same terms as full-time staff, and the rule also applies to businesses with fewer than five employees. The allowance equals (contracted weekly hours ÷ 40) × 8 × hourly wage and never exceeds 8 hours, even if you work more than 40 hours. With the {year} minimum wage of {wage}, working 4 hours a day for 5 days (20 hours) adds 4 paid hours, or {juhyu20}, every week. Overtime hours do not count toward the allowance, and a week with an unexcused absence earns none.
AlbaPay.formula: Weekly holiday allowance = (contracted weekly hours ÷ 40) × 8 × hourly wage
under5: The weekly holiday allowance still applies once you work 15 hours or more a week.
No 50% premium for overtime, night (10 pm–6 am) or holiday work — every hour is paid at the normal rate.
Hours over 8 a day or 40 a week must still be paid at your hourly wage.
Staff are counted excluding the owner; part-timers count toward the five.
break: A 4-hour shift needs at least a 30-minute break and an 8-hour shift at least one hour, given during the shift (Labor Standards Act, Article 54).
Breaks are unpaid, so 9 am to 6 pm with a one-hour lunch is 8 working hours.
The schedule tab shows a yellow note when a break is shorter than required.
excluded: Probation pay cut (90% of minimum wage for 3 months on 1-year+ contracts, not for simple labour)
Income tax from the withholding table — see the Salary Take-Home Pay Calculator
Severance pay and unused annual leave pay
Upper and lower income caps for pension and health insurance

faq.q: How many hours do I need for the weekly holiday allowance?
faq.a: You need at least 15 contracted hours a week and must attend every scheduled day that week. Three hours a day for five days (15 hours) qualifies, but seven hours on two days (14 hours) does not. It is judged week by week, and overtime does not count toward the 15 hours.

faq.q: Do small businesses with under five staff have to pay it?
faq.a: Yes. The weekly holiday allowance applies to every workplace regardless of size. What small workplaces with fewer than five regular employees skip is the 50% premium for overtime, night and holiday work, so late or long shifts are paid at the normal hourly rate there.

faq.q: What is the Korean minimum wage in {year}?
faq.a: It is {wage} an hour, up from {prevWage} in {prevYear}. For a 40-hour week the monthly equivalent is {monthly}, based on 209 paid hours (48 hours including the paid holiday × 4.345 weeks). The rate is announced around August 5 each year and applies to all workplaces from January 1.

faq.q: Should my employer deduct 4 insurances or 3.3%?
faq.a: A part-timer who works set hours under an employer's direction is an employee and is normally covered by national pension, health, employment and accident insurance. Workers under 60 hours a month may be left out of pension and health insurance. The 3.3% withholding is meant for freelancers with business income, not employees.

faq.q: When do I get the night work premium?
faq.a: Hours worked between 10 pm and 6 am earn an extra 50% of the hourly wage at workplaces with five or more staff. A 6 pm to 2 am shift includes four night hours. If those hours are also overtime beyond 8 a day, the two premiums add up to double pay.

ConcreteCalc.title: Concrete Calculator – Slabs, Footings, Columns & Bags
ConcreteCalc.subtitle: Add every pour to one list and get cubic yards, ready-mix trucks and how many bags to buy
ConcreteCalc.meta_title: Concrete Calculator – Cubic Yards, Bags & Slab Volume | Utility Hub
ConcreteCalc.meta_description: Free concrete calculator for slabs, footings, walls, round columns, fence post holes and stairs. Add several parts to one list and get cubic yards with waste, truck loads, and how many 80, 60 or 40 lb bags you need.
ConcreteCalc.description: This concrete calculator is built for jobs that are more than one simple slab. Pick a shape — slab or patio, wall or strip footing, square column or pad footing, round column or Sonotube, fence or deck post hole, stairs, or a volume you already know — and enter the dimensions in feet or inches. Each part goes into a list with its own name, so a garage slab, four pier footings and a set of front steps add up to one total. You get the net volume, the order volume with a waste allowance (5% by default, adjustable from 0 to 15%), the number of ready-mix truck loads with the size of the last load, and the approximate weight of the concrete. For small pours you can see how many 80 lb, 60 lb or 40 lb premix bags to buy, or the cement, sand and gravel for a site-mixed batch at 1:2:4, 1:3:6 or 1:1.5:3. Every input has its own unit selector, and values that look wrong — a 4-foot-thick slab, say — trigger a check-your-units warning. Copy a plain-text order summary for your supplier or print the results for a quote. Everything runs in your browser; nothing is uploaded.
ConcreteCalc.share_title: Concrete Calculator — cubic yards, trucks and bags for any pour
about: Concrete is ordered by volume, so every shape comes down to length × width × depth in the same unit. A 10 ft × 10 ft patio poured 4 inches thick is 10 × 10 × (4 ÷ 12) = 33.33 cubic feet. Divide by 27 to get cubic yards: about 1.23 yd³. The classic mistake is multiplying by 4 instead of 0.333, which makes the order twelve times too big — this calculator labels every unit and warns when a value looks unrealistic.

Round columns and Sonotubes use the area of a circle: π × radius² × height. Four 12-inch tubes 8 ft tall come to about 25.1 ft³, or 0.93 yd³. For fence and deck posts set in concrete, the post takes up part of the hole, so subtract its volume — a 4×4 post in a 10-inch hole saves roughly 15% of the concrete.

Stairs have two parts: the triangular steps (riser × tread ÷ 2 for each step) and the sloped waist slab underneath (thickness × the length of the slope). If the steps are poured solid on grade, choose “Solid fill” and the calculator uses the full stepped cross-section instead.

Add a waste allowance to the net volume to cover spillage, form bulging and uneven subgrade. Ready-mix is sold by the cubic yard and delivered in truck loads of roughly 8–10 yd³, so divide the order volume by the truck size and round up.
formula_rows: width × (steps × riser × tread ÷ 2 + waist × slope length)
4 ft wide · 4 steps (7 × 11 in) · 6 in waist ≈ 0.48 yd³
ConcreteCalc.rube_title: Cubic yards, cubic feet and m³
rube: 1 cubic yard = 27 cubic feet = 0.7646 m³. US ready-mix plants quote and deliver by the cubic yard; bagged concrete is labelled by cubic feet of yield.
A cubic yard of concrete weighs about 4,000 lb (roughly 145–150 lb per cubic foot). Keep this in mind for trailer loads, wheelbarrow trips and suspended forms.
Truck size: a full mixer usually carries 8–10 yd³, and many suppliers charge a short-load fee below a minimum. Ask your plant — the truck size in this calculator is editable.
waste: Formed slabs and footings: 5%. Straight forms and a level, compacted base. This is the default.
Slabs on uneven ground: 5–10%. Low spots in the subgrade eat concrete fast — a half-inch dip across a 20 × 20 ft slab is about 0.6 yd³.
Post holes and dug footings: 10–15%. Holes are rarely perfectly round and the walls cave in a little.
Running short means waiting for another truck and risking a cold joint, so round up when in doubt.
ConcreteCalc.mix_title: Premix bags vs. mixing your own
mix: Premix bags already contain cement, sand and gravel. Typical yields are 0.60 ft³ for an 80 lb bag, 0.45 ft³ for 60 lb and 0.30 ft³ for 40 lb, so one cubic yard takes about 45 bags of 80 lb.

Site mixing at 1 : 2 : 4 (cement : sand : gravel) is the general-purpose ratio for slabs, footings and posts. 1 : 3 : 6 is for blinding and non-structural fill; 1 : 1.5 : 3 is stronger and uses the most cement.

Dry ingredients shrink when mixed, so the calculator multiplies the wet volume by 1.54, converts cement at 1,440 kg/m³ (about 90 lb/ft³) and counts 94 lb bags of Portland cement. Water is estimated at half the cement weight.
Past roughly one cubic yard, ready-mix is usually cheaper and far less work than bags.
ConcreteCalc.excluded_title: What this calculator does not cover
excluded: Rebar, mesh and formwork area are not calculated.
It does not design a mix for a specific strength (e.g. 3,000 or 4,000 psi) — specify that when you order ready-mix.
Sloped or irregular shapes: split them into rectangles and add each one as a part.
Prices, minimum orders and short-load fees vary by supplier, so none are built in.

faq.q: How many bags of concrete do I need for a 10×10 slab?
faq.a: A 10 × 10 ft slab 4 inches thick is 33.33 cubic feet, or about 1.23 cubic yards. With 80 lb bags yielding 0.60 ft³ each that is 56 bags, or 75 bags of 60 lb. Add 5–10% for waste, and for anything over about a yard compare the price of a ready-mix delivery before buying that many bags.

faq.q: How many 80 lb bags make a cubic yard?
faq.a: About 45. A cubic yard is 27 cubic feet and an 80 lb bag of premix yields roughly 0.60 cubic feet, so 27 ÷ 0.60 = 45 bags. With 60 lb bags it is about 60, and with 40 lb bags about 90. Yields vary slightly by brand, so check the number printed on the bag.

faq.q: How much concrete do I need for a fence post?
faq.a: Calculate the hole volume and subtract the post. A 10-inch hole 3 feet deep holds about 1.64 ft³; a 4×4 post (3.5 × 3.5 in actual) takes up about 0.26 ft³, leaving roughly 1.38 ft³. That is about 2.3 bags of 80 lb, so plan on three 80 lb bags (or four 60 lb bags) per post.

faq.q: How much extra concrete should I order?
faq.a: Order 5% extra for formed slabs and footings on a level base, 5–10% for slabs on uneven ground, and 10–15% for dug post holes and footings. Running short means a second delivery, possible short-load fees and a cold joint where the two pours meet, which is weaker and can crack.

faq.q: How much does a yard of concrete weigh?
faq.a: Normal-weight concrete weighs about 145–150 pounds per cubic foot, so a cubic yard is roughly 3,900–4,050 pounds — close to two tons. That is why a typical pickup truck can only carry about half a yard of mixed concrete safely, and why suspended forms need solid shoring.

SlingCalc.title: Sling Angle & Rigging Load Calculator
SlingCalc.subtitle: Enter the load and the sling angle to see the real tension in each leg and whether it stays within the sling’s WLL
SlingCalc.meta_title: Sling Angle Calculator – Rigging Load & Leg Tension | Utility Hub
SlingCalc.meta_description: Free sling angle calculator: enter the load, number of legs (1–4) and the angle from horizontal, vertical, included angle or leg lengths to get tension per leg, the load angle factor and a pass/fail check against the sling WLL. lb, US ton and metric units.
SlingCalc.description: This sling angle calculator works out the tension in each sling leg from the load weight and the rigging angle. Lift 20,000 lb on two legs hanging straight down and each leg carries 10,000 lb. Open the legs to 60° from horizontal and each leg carries 11,547 lb; at 45° it is 14,142 lb, and at 30° from horizontal each leg carries the full 20,000 lb. The flatter the legs, the more they pull against each other sideways, and that horizontal pull adds to the tension. You can enter the angle from horizontal (the "sling angle" used in OSHA and ASME charts), the angle from vertical, the included angle between the legs, or simply the leg length and horizontal distance if you cannot measure the angle. Add the working load limit (WLL) from the sling tag and the result turns green or red with the percentage of WLL used. For 3- and 4-leg bridles the calculator assumes only two legs carry the load by default, because unequal leg lengths rarely let every leg share evenly. Units include lb, US (short) tons, metric tons, kg and kN, clearly labelled so a short ton is never confused with a metric ton. Nothing is sent to a server; your inputs stay on this device.
SlingCalc.share_title: Sling Angle Calculator – tension per leg in seconds
SlingCalc.about_title: How sling angle changes the load on each leg
about: When sling legs hang straight down, the load simply divides between them. Once the legs spread out, each leg must hold up its share of the weight and also resist the sideways pull of the other leg. That is why the same load puts more tension on each leg as the angle opens up.

Leg tension = load ÷ (number of legs sharing × cos θ), where θ is the angle between a leg and the vertical. The multiplier 1 ÷ cos θ is the load angle factor: 1.155 at 60° from horizontal, 1.414 at 45° and 2.000 at 30°.

At 30° from horizontal (120° between the legs) each leg carries the entire load even though there are two of them. At 15° from horizontal the factor jumps to 3.86. ASME B30.9 does not allow horizontal sling angles below 30° unless the sling manufacturer or a qualified person approves, and most riggers aim for 60° or steeper.

To steepen the angle, use longer legs, bring the pick points closer together, or use a spreader or lifting beam. The same sling choked up short can easily exceed its WLL, so check the tension at the actual angle before the lift.
SlingCalc.factor_note: Load factor = 1 ÷ sin(angle from horizontal) = 1 ÷ cos(angle from vertical). From 30° above horizontal and flatter, each leg carries at least the full load.
SlingCalc.why4_title: Why not divide a 4-leg lift by four?
why4: Four legs rarely share a load evenly. A few millimetres of difference in leg length or pick-point height lets two legs take up first while the others stay slack.
This is especially true for rigid loads such as steel, precast blocks and dies. Dividing by four can put the calculated tension at about half the real value and lead to an undersized sling.

So this calculator assumes only two legs carry the load on 3- and 4-leg bridles — the most conservative choice. You can switch to three legs sharing, the basis European standard EN 13414 uses, but stay with two if the load is rigid or the legs are not matched exactly.
apex: Angle from horizontal is measured between a leg and the top of the load. It is the "sling angle" in OSHA and ASME charts, so most US rigging tables use it.
Angle from vertical is measured between a leg and a plumb line from the hook. It equals 90° minus the horizontal angle.
Included angle is the angle between two legs at the hook — twice the vertical angle. A 60° horizontal angle equals a 30° vertical angle and a 60° included angle.

Can’t measure the angle? Enter the leg length and the horizontal distance from the hook centre to the pick point. A 12 ft leg with 6 ft horizontal distance is 30° from vertical, or 60° from horizontal.
law: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.184 (general industry) and 1926.251 (construction) require slings to be used within their rated capacity and inspected before use; damaged slings must be removed from service.

Sling capacity tables in OSHA and ASME B30.9 already include the effect of sling angle for bridle hitches. If you use those tables, look up the angle; if you use a single-leg WLL, compare it with the leg tension shown here.
Rated capacity on the tag already includes the manufacturer’s design factor (typically 5:1 for wire rope and 4:1 for alloy chain). Do not divide it again.
Standards are summarised for orientation only, as checked in November 2026. Follow the current regulation and your company lift plan.
SlingCalc.excluded_title: What this version does not cover
excluded: Off-centre centre of gravity — the leg closer to the centre of gravity carries more.
Legs of different lengths — the shorter leg sits steeper and takes more load.
Choker and basket hitch reduction or increase factors
Dynamic loading — sudden stops, swinging and wind raise the peak tension.
Lifts using spreader beams or lifting beams

use_cases.desc: Before picking a 7,000 lb skid on two legs at 45° from horizontal, a rigger confirms each leg sees about 4,950 lb and that a 4,000 lb sling would be overloaded.

use_cases.title: Shipyard and plant lifts
use_cases.desc: On a four-leg bridle the calculator uses two legs sharing instead of four, so the sling chosen still holds when leg lengths are not perfectly matched.

use_cases.title: Rigging training
use_cases.desc: Drag the slider from 90° down to 15° from horizontal and watch the factor climb from 1.0 to 3.86 on the chart and diagram — an easy way to teach why flat angles are dangerous.

use_cases.desc: A safety lead enters the load, legs and angle from a lift plan, checks the percentage of WLL used, and pastes the one-line result into the review notes as the calculation basis.

how_to.desc: Type the load weight and pick lb, US ton (2,000 lb), metric t (1,000 kg), kg or kN. Decimals like 2.5 are fine.
Pick 1 to 4 legs. Three- and four-leg bridles assume two legs carry the load unless you switch to three under the sharing option.
Use the angle from horizontal, from vertical or the included angle with the number box or slider. If you cannot measure it, switch to Lengths and enter leg length and horizontal distance.
Enter the single-leg vertical WLL from the tag to see the percentage used and a green or red verdict. Copy the result to share it with your crew.

faq.q: Why does a 30° sling angle double the tension?
faq.a: At 30° from horizontal, each leg is 60° from vertical and cos 60° = 0.5. Tension = load ÷ (2 × 0.5), which equals the full load, so a 20,000 lb lift on two legs puts 20,000 lb on each leg. The flatter the legs, the harder they pull against each other sideways, and below 30° the tension rises very quickly.

faq.q: Why not divide a four-leg lift by four?
faq.a: Small differences in leg length or pick-point height mean two legs usually take most of the load, especially with rigid loads. The calculator therefore assumes two legs by default, with an option for three legs sharing as in EN 13414. It never divides by four.

faq.q: Which WLL should I enter from the sling tag?
faq.a: Enter the single-leg vertical rated capacity. The calculator already applies the angle to the leg tension, so using the tag’s bridle rating at a given angle would count the angle twice. Choker and basket hitch ratings are not part of this check.

faq.q: Is a US ton the same as a metric ton?
faq.a: No. A US (short) ton is 2,000 lb and a metric ton is 1,000 kg, or 2,204.62 lb — about 10% more. Mixing them up can understate the load by 10%, so the unit list labels them separately as "US ton" and "metric t".

faq.q: If the tension is within the WLL, is the lift safe?
faq.a: Not by itself. The result is a static calculation that leaves out shock loading, off-centre loads, unequal legs and hitch reduction factors. If you are above about 90% of WLL, consider the next size up, and always follow the manufacturer’s rating, a qualified rigger and your lift plan.
